# Best Practices, starting template

`blog-system-install` starts from this file, confirms the word count and any
business-specific rules with the owner, and writes the result into the business's
Drive folder. `blog-writer` treats the resulting doc as the authority on structure.

The owner can edit their copy at any time. Everything below is a default, not a law.

## Length

- Target: 1,200 words unless the owner set a different number
- Acceptable range: within roughly ten percent of target
- Do not pad to hit a count. A tight 900 words beats a bloated 1,300.

## Structure

- One `H1`, the article title, containing the primary keyword phrase
- `H2` for major sections, `H3` only when an H2 genuinely subdivides
- Never skip a level, no H3 sitting directly under an H1
- **Use real heading styles**, not bold text sized up. Bold is not a heading and
  carries no SEO weight. In a Google Doc that means the actual Heading 1, Heading 2,
  and Heading 3 styles.
- Two to four sentences per paragraph, and single-sentence paragraphs are fine for
  emphasis
- **A section running past roughly 150 words gets a subhead or a list**

## Opening

- Answer the reader's question, or promise to, in the first two sentences
- **Primary keyword phrase in the first sentence or two**, worked in naturally. Not
  merely somewhere in the first hundred words. A reader and a crawler both decide
  what the page is about from the opening lines.
- At least one concrete, cited number in the opening
- No "in today's fast-paced world," no dictionary definitions, no throat clearing

## Scannability

Skimmability is a ranking factor and a reading factor. Lean on lists rather than
avoiding them.

- **Any paragraph that is really a list becomes a list**
- Bullets for parallel items, numbers only for genuine sequences
- Bold the term being defined, not whole sentences
- A table when comparing three or more things on two or more attributes
- Assume a reader who skims the whole page first and reads second. Long unbroken
  prose loses that reader before the call to action.

## Keywords

- Primary phrase: the title, the H1, **the first sentence or two**, and one or two
  subheads where it fits the sentence
- **Supporting phrases carry real weight.** Each one should own a section, a subhead,
  or at minimum a sentence written to answer that specific query. They are longer and
  less contested than the primary, which is why they earn traffic the primary never
  will. They are not synonyms to sprinkle in.
- Do not build post after post on the same one or two head terms. Articles competing
  for the same results page cannibalize each other.
- If a phrase has to be bent into a sentence, drop it. Stuffing costs more in
  rankings than the placement gains, and costs more again in whether a human keeps
  reading.

## Meta fields

- `Meta Title`: 50 to 60 characters, primary phrase near the front, business name
  only if it fits
- `Meta Description`: 150 to 160 characters, one concrete reason to click, active
  voice
- `URL Slug`: lowercase, hyphen separated, three to five words, no stop words, no
  dates

## Linking

**Internal links, at every reasonable opportunity.** This is one of the
highest-leverage on-page moves available and it costs nothing.

- Link to relevant published articles, service pages, product pages, and the contact
  page
- Three to six internal links in a normal-length article is a healthy range
- Only real, published, live URLs. Never a Google Doc, never a draft that is not
  published, never a guessed URL.
- Descriptive anchor text carrying the target page's topic, never "click here" and
  never a bare URL

**Outbound links to sources**, per the Citations section below. Primary sources, not
competitors.

## Quantitative bias

Numbers outperform adjectives with human readers, with rankings, and with AI
Overviews and answer engines, which lift concrete figures and skip vague claims.

- Prefer a specific cited figure over a qualitative assertion. "Cuts setup time by
  roughly 40 percent, per the 2025 industry survey" beats "saves significant time."
- Include counts, percentages, dollar ranges, timeframes, and dates wherever the
  subject allows one
- Several supported figures per article, at least one in the opening
- **Never invent a number to satisfy this.** An unsourced statistic is worse than no
  statistic. If a figure cannot be found and cited, write the sentence qualitatively.

## Citations and accuracy

Every fact, statistic, price, date, or characterization of an outside party carries
an inline link to its source.

- Link on descriptive anchor text at the point of the claim, not in a footnote pile
- Prefer primary sources: the study, the government page, the company's own
  documentation. Not a blog summarizing a study.
- Verify by searching rather than recalling. If no source can be found, cut the claim.
- Never invent a customer quote, review, or testimonial
- Leave out a claim that cannot be supported, rather than hedging it

This does three jobs at once: outbound links to authoritative sources are good SEO, a
reviewer can check accuracy in minutes rather than an hour, and it makes the
fabricated-statistic failure mode structurally hard.

## Voice

- The Voice doc governs. Where this document and the Voice doc conflict, the Voice
  doc wins.
- No em dashes. Commas, periods, or parentheses.
- Second person for instructions, first person for the business's own perspective
- No exclamation points unless the Voice doc shows the owner using them

## Closing

- End with the call to action if the business chose that option, worded around the
  target action
- One clear next step, not three competing ones

## Business-specific rules

*The installer fills this section from its interview: claims the business cannot
legally make, terminology they insist on, competitors they will not name,
regulatory language they must include.*
